about: THE RIDDLES - real riddles and wisdom questions with their answers as the sources give them or scholars agree; "answers": the things (palette) that answer each, dragged onto it; "acquire": where and how it is had; "wakeOn": what, newly learned, wakes it when it rests; "rewards" and "sets". The words round them are yours to write.

angelica (a tall herb of the North)

riddles.answerSource: the saga: King Heidrek's prose solution, as given in English by CPB p. 87
clues: Would I had what I had yesterday!
Men’s damager
words’ hinderer
and yet words’ arouser
riddles.notes: The first riddle in all versions. Every riddle ends with the refrain 'Heiðrekr konungr hygg þú at gꜵ́to!' ('Read my riddle, O King Heidrek!'); CPB shortens it after no. 1 to 'H. k. h.' and 'Read my, etc.'. Links to Alvis's lay st. 33-34 (the names of ale).

acquire.why: He keeps to the old gods and knows the hall riddles; this is the first of the old contest (first in every version).

way underneath, way above head, way on all sides

acquire.why: A smith's riddle about his own hammer (metal workshops at Ribe and Hedeby).

swallowing water and woods
he fears the wind, but no man
wages war on the sun

turning half towards Hell
he saves people, but tugs against the earth
if he has a trusty withy by him

acquire.why: Skalds were paid in silver for verse; four questions on one stick.

riddles.notes: Part 2 of 4 of riddle 7. Compare Vafthruthnir's lay st. 14: 'thence come the dews in the dales'.

acquire.who: a skald at the king's seat

riddles.notes: Part 3 of 4 of riddle 7.

acquire.who: a skald at the king's seat
acquire.why: On the same stick as r-gest-07a.

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 88

riddles.notes: Part 4 of 4 of riddle 7. 'Fall' means a waterfall.

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 88
clues: outside Delling’s door (outside the hall)
It turns its head towards Hell
and its feet towards the Sun
riddles.notes: The bulb points down, the leaves up. 'Delling's door' (riddles 8-16): Delling is the father of Day (Vafthruthnir's lay st. 25), so 'outside Delling's door' means out of doors by day. A chain: that stanza explains the phrase.

acquire.why: Delling's door follows from the lore of Delling: the chain leads here.

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 88
clues: Two ever-stirring yet lifeless things
boiling a wound-leek
sára-lauk
riddles.notes: 'Wound-leek' (sára-laukr) is a kenning for a sword: a kenning to decode first. CPB footnote to l. 35: B reads 'okvikvir'.

acquire.why: The bellows and the sword he forges are his daily work.

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 88
clues: The white flyers beat the rock
while the black ones are embedded in the sand
riddles.notes: Hauksbók only (B omits it, CPB p. 87).

acquire.why: Weather lore passes between seamen.

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 89
clues: a black hog wallow in the mud
though no bristles were on his back
riddles.notes: Hauksbók only (B omits it, CPB p. 87).

acquire.who: a cattle drover at the market
acquire.why: A pasture riddle; he walks behind the herds.

riddles.answer: A sow with a litter of nine pigs.
riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 89
clues: It has ten tongues, twenty eyes, forty feet
this being moves along
riddles.notes: Counting puzzle: ten animals walking together. CPB footnote to l. 48: 'fram líðr] B; fer hart, A.'

acquire.who: a swineherd of the king's estate
acquire.why: He keeps the king's pigs.

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 89
clues: It flies high aloft
yelling loud
‘arn-hlióð’ gellr
riddles.notes: The verse is damaged: CPB prints 'harðar ro hilmir' . . . and no English for the rest.

acquire.who: a broken stick in the rubbish of the craft quarter
acquire.why: Rune sticks were thrown out with a town's rubbish; this one is broken (the gaps in the text).

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 89
clues: It has eight feet, four eyes
carrying its knees higher than its belly

acquire.why: A weaver's riddle about another weaver.

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 89
clues: It lightens people over all lands
and yet is ever chased by wolves
riddles.notes: Hauksbók only (B omits it, CPB p. 87). The wolf that snatches the sun: Vafthruthnir's lay st. 46-47. Sky things are filed under 'weather' here.

acquire.who: a Rus trader on the Volkhov
acquire.why: Rune sticks with verse are known from Aldeigjuborg (9th c.) (?).

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 89
clues: Harder than horn
blacker than a raven
whiter than egg-film
straighter than a shaft
riddles.notes: CPB gives two choices; the saga's own Norse prose was not checked here (?).

acquire.why: Raven-flint (obsidian) comes from Iceland, settled from 874 (?).

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 89
clues: Blond-haired brides, bondswomen both
carried ale to the barn
the casks were not turned with hands, nor forged by hammers
she that made it strutted about outside the isles
riddles.notes: The casks are the eggshells, the ale inside them the egg; the maker is the eider duck on the islands.

acquire.who: a fowler from the outer skerries
acquire.why: He gathers eider eggs and down on the islands.

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 90
clues: those fairies of the mighty mountains
woman begets by a woman
a maid bears a son by a maid
Those goodwives have no husband
riddles.notes: Angelica is a tall plant of the North (Norse hvǫnn). Whether the game has it as a good is the user's call (?).

acquire.who: a farm wife with an angelica bed
acquire.why: Angelica was grown and eaten in the Norse west (?).

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 90
clues: the maids that fight weaponless around their lord
the brown ever sheltering
the fair ever attacking him
riddles.notes: The lord is the king piece of hnefatafl. Ties to the board games plan (map_play.md B2). See also riddles 25 and 31.

acquire.who: a man of Birka's garrison with a gaming bag; later, a Danish warrior at Sliesthorp
acquire.why: Birka grave Bj 581 held tafl pieces and dice (mid-900s).

riddles.answer: Snow-flakes and rain [the text gives Rep-hens (!)].
riddles.answerSource: the saga's prose gives ptarmigans ('Rep-hens'); CPB p. 90 prefers its own guess, snow-flakes and rain
clues: the merry maids that glide above the land
to the joy of their father
in winter they bear a white shield, but black in summer
riddles.notes: Accept the saga's answer, the ptarmigan (white in winter, dark in summer). CPB's Final Readings (p. cxxvi) change l. 79 to 'hvítar váðir þær of vetrom bera: en svartar u. s.' ('white clothes in winter, black in summer'), which suits the bird. agreed=true is for the saga's answer only.

acquire.why: He snares ptarmigan in winter.

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 90
clues: the maids that go weeping to the joy of their father
white-hooded, fair-haired
wide awake in a gale
riddles.notes: Riddles 21, 22 and 23 have the same answer: a set of three. CPB p. 87: 'several have the same answer'. Their father is the sea. CPB footnote 78: 'fögnuði] emend.; forvitni, Cd.'

acquire.why: The sea's riddles are seamen's.

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 90 ('The same' = the waves)
clues: the maids that go many together
to the joy of their father
they have brought grief to many
these goodwives have no husbands
riddles.notes: Second of the three wave riddles (21-23). CPB prints B's different wording in its footnote to ll. 85 ff.

acquire.why: Skalds were paid in silver for verse.

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 90 ('The same' = the waves)
clues: the brides that walk over the reefs
drive along the friths
these white-hooded ladies have a hard bed
in calm weather they make no stir
riddles.notes: Third of the three wave riddles (21-23).

acquire.why: He works the water every day.

riddles.answer: A dead horse floated on an icefloe.
riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 91
clues: an earth-dweller pass by
a corpse sitting on a corpse
a blind one riding on a blind sea-car
yet the steed was lifeless
riddles.notes: CPB footnotes: '95. til] somehow wrong; a noun is required (icefloe)' and '94. nár á ná] A; naðr á nai, B' (B: an adder on a corpse). Line 2 is cited in Snorri's Skáldskaparmál (CPB p. 87).

acquire.who: a Rus trader who winters on the Volkhov
acquire.why: The Volkhov's ice breaks up each spring and carries what lies on it (?).

riddles.answer: The húnn (bear) or headpiece in the game of hnef-tafl (fox and geese).
riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 91
clues: all girdled with iron
which kills the flocks
it has eight horns, but no head
riddles.notes: The last line is lost in A ('ok . . .'); CPB footnotes: '98. iarni kringr utan, B' and '100. ok fylgia þvi margir miok, B'. The tafl set again (see 19, 31).

acquire.who: a noble guest of the monastery (the monks won't stake); later, a Dublin woodcarver selling pegged boards
acquire.why: A glass gaming piece of the 700s-800s was found at Lindisfarne; the Ballinderry board (900s) is thought Dublin work (?). The stick is broken (the gap in the text).

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 91

with bloody back it covers men
encounters spears
saves many a life
fitting its body to the hands of men
riddles.notes: CPB footnote: '104. lófa] B; lofða, A.'

acquire.who: a warrior of the Danish king's following
acquire.why: A warrior's riddle about his shield (Godfred brought his host to Sliesthorp in 804).

riddles.answer: A duck building her nest in a neat’s head with the horns on.
riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 91
clues: yearning for children
gathered her building materials
straw-choppers fenced her in
above her was drink’s echoing hall
riddles.notes: A neat is an ox. The first line is damaged (CPB: 'A . . . .'). 'Drink's echoing hall' fits the horns (drinking horns) and 'straw-choppers' the ox's teeth (?). CPB Final Readings (p. cxxvi): '108. þó lá drykkjar dryn-rann yfir?'

acquire.who: a broken stick in the hall's midden
acquire.why: Rune sticks were thrown out with the rubbish; this one is broken (the gaps in the text).

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 91
clues: Four ganging, four hanging
two showing the way
two keeping the dogs off
one ever dirty lags behind
riddles.notes: Legs, teats, eyes, horns, tail (?).

riddles.answer: A spark hidden in a flint.
riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 91
clues: sleeps in the hearth
all made of stone
a mischievous being without father or mother
there is his lifelong abode
riddles.notes: CPB footnotes: '112. avs grva, B' and '114. fagr-giarni, B'.

acquire.why: Fire and flint are a smith's daily stuff.

riddles.answer: A loom (the upright) worked by a woman.
riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 91
clues: I saw a horse
a maid whipped it
she shook a
riddles.notes: Hauksbók only (B omits it, CPB p. 87). The text is damaged and CPB leaves part untranslated; CPB footnote '116. meri] read mær?'.

acquire.who: a broken stick among the weavers' houses
acquire.why: Rune sticks were thrown out with the rubbish; this one is broken (the gaps in the text).

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 92
clues: the champions riding to court sixteen together
they send their men far and wide to make settlements
riddles.notes: Sixteen pieces on a board. CPB footnote: '120. sáttir allir sam, B.' The tafl set (see 19, 25).

acquire.who: the steward of a chief's hall
acquire.why: The Gokstad ship (c. 900) held a two-sided gaming board (Vestfold).

riddles.answer: A sow with a litter of sucking pigs.
riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 92
clues: a household awake and merry at sunset
the gentlemen drank their beer in silence
but the ale-butt stood and screamed
riddles.notes: Same answer family as riddle 12.

acquire.who: a Gotland farmer at the market
acquire.why: A farm riddle.

riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 92
clues: certain dust-like maidens
the rocks were their bedding
black and swart in sunshine
the less one can see [i. e. in the dark] the fairer they look
riddles.notes: Hauksbók only (B omits it, CPB p. 87).

acquire.who: the woman who keeps the hall's hearth
acquire.why: She banks the hall's fire each night.

riddles.answer: A pun, (a hearth, a hawk, a duck, talons.)
riddles.answerSource: CPB p. 92 and its footnotes a-d; CPB p. 87 says this riddle 'has not been read before; it depends on an intricate pun'
clues: árinn = a hearth, also a stone wall
egg-dauða menn = valr, the slain, also a hawk
blood-tube = æðr, a vein, also a duck
belly’s birch = talons
riddles.notes: Each phrase has two meanings: valr is 'the slain' and 'hawk', æðr is 'vein' and 'eider duck'. Read the second meanings: a hawk with a duck in its talons. The clues are CPB's footnotes, not the verse; show them only as hints. CPB's verse is its own emendation; the manuscripts read 'Sat eg a segli sa eg dauða menn bloðs hold bera í bork viðar (!)'. agreed=true rests on CPB alone; the saga's own prose solution was not checked here (?).

acquire.why: Word-play on two meanings was the skald's craft.
acquire.needs: standing 'known' (30) or better at the hall

riddles.answer: The one-eyed Woden riding Sleipni his eight-legged steed.
riddles.answerSource: the saga: Heidrek's prose solution, as given by CPB p. 92
clues: the two that have ten feet, three eyes, one tail
riddles.notes: Needs Odin lore: one eye, an eight-legged horse. In the saga the asker is Odin himself.

acquire.why: He carves the picture stones that show a rider on an eight-legged horse (?).

riddles.answer: Skinfaxi is he, the steed who for men / The glittering day doth draw
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Othin's answer, st. 12 (text t-vafth-12)
clues: What name has the steed
that each morn anew
The day for mankind doth draw
riddles.notes: The giant asks; Othin, calling himself Gagnrath, answers. Bellows: 'Skinfaxi: Shining-Mane.'

acquire.why: The giant's questions in the wisdom contest are hall lore.

riddles.answer: Hrimfaxi name they the steed that anew / Brings night for the noble gods
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Othin's answer, st. 14 (text t-vafth-14)
clues: What name has the steed
that from East anew
Brings night for the noble gods
riddles.notes: Bellows: 'Hrimfaxi: Frosty-Mane.' St. 14 says the foam from his bit is the dew in the dales (links to Gestumblindi 3 and 7b).

acquire.why: The giant's questions in the wisdom contest are hall lore.

riddles.answer: Ifing is the river that ’twixt the realms / Of the gods and the giants goes
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Othin's answer, st. 16 (text t-vafth-16)
clues: What name has the river
that ’twixt the realms / Of the gods and the giants goes
riddles.notes: Bellows: no other reference to this river, which never freezes, so the giants cannot cross it.

acquire.who: a skald of the Svear king
acquire.why: The giant's questions in the wisdom contest are hall lore.

riddles.answer: Vigrith is the field where in fight shall meet / Surt and the gracious gods
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Othin's answer, st. 18 (text t-vafth-18)
clues: What name has the field
where in fight shall meet / Surt and the gracious gods
riddles.notes: Bellows: 'Vigrith: the Field of Battle.' A hundred miles each way.

acquire.who: a skald of the Svear king
acquire.why: The giant's questions in the wisdom contest are hall lore.

riddles.answer: Out of Ymir’s flesh was fashioned the earth, / And the mountains were made of his bones; / The sky from the frost-cold giant’s skull, / And the ocean out of his blood.
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 21 (text t-vafth-21)
clues: In earliest time whence came the earth
Or the sky
riddles.notes: Ymir is the first giant. Othin's first question. 'person' here covers giants and other named beings.

acquire.who: a skald of the Norse king's hall
acquire.why: Norse kings held York and Dublin, with their skalds (Egill at York: told later).

riddles.answer: Mundilferi is he who begat the moon, / And fathered the flaming sun
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 23 (text t-vafth-23)
clues: Whence came the moon
and the flaming sun
riddles.notes: Bellows: known only as the father of Mani (the Moon) and Sol (the Sun).

acquire.who: a skald of the Svear king
acquire.why: Odin's questions in the wisdom contest are hall lore.

riddles.answer: The father of day is Delling called, / And the night was begotten by Nor
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 25 (text t-vafth-25)
clues: Whence came the day
Or night with the narrowing moon
riddles.notes: Two answers in one. Delling explains 'outside Delling's door' in Gestumblindi's riddles 8-16: a chain.

acquire.who: a skald of the Svear king
acquire.why: Odin's questions in the wisdom contest are hall lore.

riddles.answer: Vindsval he was who was winter’s father, / And Svosuth summer begat
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 27 (text t-vafth-27)
clues: Whence did winter come
or the summer warm
riddles.notes: Two answers. St. 27 is half lost. Bellows: 'Vindsval: the Wind-Cold'; 'Svosuth: the Gentle'.

acquire.why: Winter and summer winds are a seaman's lore.

riddles.answer: Winters unmeasured ere earth was made / Was the birth of Bergelmir; / Thruthgelmir’s son was the giant strong, / And Aurgelmir’s grandson of old.
riddles.answerSource: the poem, st. 29 (text t-vafth-29), with Bellows' note 29: 'Aurgelmir was the frost-giants’ name for Ymir himself. Thus Ymir was the first of the giants, and so Othin’s question is answered.'
clues: What giant first was fashioned of old
the eldest of Ymir’s kin
riddles.notes: The stanza names three generations; the eldest is the grandfather, Aurgelmir, who is Ymir. Answer by reading the family line, not the first name given.

acquire.who: a skald of the Dublin kings
acquire.why: The next question of the giant's line: the chain leads here.

riddles.answer: Down from Elivagar did venom drop, / And waxed till a giant it was
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 31 (text t-vafth-31)
clues: Whence did Aurgelmir come
with the giants’ kin
riddles.notes: Bellows: 'Elivagar (Stormy Waves)'; the last two lines of st. 31 are from Snorri's version, as both manuscripts omit them.

acquire.who: the master of a Dublin ship you hail on the Irish Sea
acquire.why: Ships ran between Dublin and York by the Ribble and the Mersey (?).

riddles.answer: They say ’neath the arms of the giant of ice / Grew man-child and maid together; / And foot with foot did the wise one fashion / A son that six heads bore.
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 33 (text t-vafth-33)
clues: How begat he children
Who never a giantess knew
riddles.notes: Bellows: Snorri says the son and daughter were born under Ymir's left arm.

acquire.who: a skald of the York kings
acquire.why: The next question of the giant's line: the chain leads here.

riddles.answer: This first knew I well, when the giant wise / In a boat of old was borne.
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 35 (text t-vafth-35)
clues: What farthest back dost thou bear in mind?
riddles.notes: The Norse word is lúþr; Bellows has 'boat', CPB (vol. 1 p. 66) 'laid in the Ark'. The word's meaning is argued (?). Bellows note 29: Bergelmir and his wife escaped the flood of Ymir's blood in a boat.

acquire.why: Norse-Gaels kept the old lore beside the new faith (Olaf Cuaran of Dublin and York ended his days at Iona, 980).

riddles.answer: In an eagle’s guise at the end of heaven / Hræsvelg sits, they say; / And from his wings does the wind come forth
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 37 (text t-vafth-37)
clues: Whence comes the wind
that fares o’er the waves
Yet never itself is seen
riddles.notes: Hræsvelg is a giant in eagle form; Bellows: 'the Corpse-Eater'. A sailor's question: where the wind comes from.

acquire.why: Where the wind comes from is a seaman's question.

riddles.answer: In the home of the Wanes did the wise ones create him, / And gave him as pledge to the gods
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 39 (text t-vafth-39)
clues: Whence came up Njorth to the kin of the gods
Though of gods he was never begot
riddles.notes: Bellows: the Wanes gave Njorth as a hostage to the gods at the end of their war. Norse: 'Í Vanaheimi'.

acquire.who: a skald of the Svear king
acquire.why: The Svear honoured the Wanes' gods at Uppsala (Adam of Bremen, 1070s: told later).

riddles.answer: The heroes all in Othin’s hall / Each day to fight go forth; / They fell each other, and fare from the fight / All healed full soon to sit.
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 41 (text t-vafth-41)
clues: What men
Each day to fight go forth
riddles.notes: St. 40 is damaged in both manuscripts. Bellows' note 40 suggests: 'Eleventh answer me well, if thou knowest all / The fate that is fixed for the gods: / What men are they who in Othin’s home / Each day to fight go forth?' The Norse 'einherjar' are the heroes brought to Valhall by the Valkyries (Bellows note 41).

acquire.who: a broken stick in the hall's midden
acquire.why: Stanza 40 is damaged in both manuscripts: here the stick is broken.

riddles.answer: To nine worlds came I, to Niflhel beneath, / The home where dead men dwell.
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 43 (text t-vafth-43)
clues: Twelfth answer me now how all thou knowest
Of the runes of the gods and the giants’ race
riddles.notes: The question is how he knows: he has been in all nine worlds. Bellows: 'Niflhel: Dark-Hell.'

acquire.who: a skald of the Svear king
acquire.why: Odin's questions in the wisdom contest are hall lore.

riddles.answer: In Hoddmimir’s wood shall hide themselves / Lif and Lifthrasir then
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 45 (text t-vafth-45)
clues: What shall live of mankind
The mighty winter to men
riddles.notes: Bellows: Lif ('Life') and Lifthrasir, from whom the new race of men will spring; they live on the morning dews.

acquire.why: Odin's questions in the wisdom contest are hall lore.

riddles.answer: A daughter bright Alfrothul bears / Ere Fenrir snatches her forth
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 47 (text t-vafth-47)
clues: Whence comes the sun to the smooth sky back
When Fenrir has snatched it forth
riddles.notes: Bellows: 'Alfrothul (the Elf-Beam): the sun.' Links to Gestumblindi 15 (the sun chased by wolves).

acquire.why: After the sun chased by wolves: the chain leads here.

riddles.answer: O’er Mogthrasir’s hill shall the maidens pass, / And three are their throngs that come; / They all shall protect the dwellers on earth
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 49 (text t-vafth-49)
clues: What maidens are they, so wise of mind
That forth o’er the sea shall fare
riddles.notes: Bellows: apparently Norns, kindly to men. The Norse calls them 'hamingjur' (guardian spirits).

acquire.who: a skald at the king's seat
acquire.why: Odin's questions in the wisdom contest are hall lore.

riddles.answer: In the gods’ home Vithar and Vali shall dwell, / When the fires of Surt have sunk; / Mothi and Magni shall Mjollnir have
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 51 (text t-vafth-51)
clues: Who then shall rule the realm of the gods
When the fires of Surt have sunk
riddles.notes: Four gods in the answer: Vithar and Vali dwell in the gods' home; Mothi and Magni, Thor's sons, get his hammer (Bellows note 51). Could be split into parts.

acquire.why: Odin's questions in the wisdom contest are hall lore.

riddles.answer: The wolf shall fell the father of men, / And this shall Vithar avenge
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Vafthruthnir's answer, st. 53 (text t-vafth-53)
clues: What shall bring the doom of death to Othin
riddles.notes: Bellows: 'The wolf: Fenrir.'

acquire.who: a skald of the Svear king
acquire.why: The wolf of the sun's daughter: the chain ends at the Svear kings' seat.

riddles.answer: What call they the earth, that lies before all
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Thor's question, st. 9 (text t-alv-09)
clues: ‘Field’ to the gods
‘The Ways’ is it called by the Wanes
‘Ever Green’ by the giants
‘The Grower’ by elves
‘The Moist’ by the holy ones high
riddles.notes: The poem goes the other way: Thor names the thing, Alvis gives its names. Here the answer stanza is the riddle and the thing is dragged; the men's word gives it away, so hide it (the user's call). 'names' lists each world's word for the hall-lore form ('What do the giants call the earth?').

acquire.who: a skald at the king's seat
acquire.why: Skalds needed many names for one thing; he knows them by heart.

riddles.answer: What call they the heaven, beheld of the high one
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Thor's question, st. 11 (text t-alv-11)
clues: ‘The Height’ the gods
The Wanes ‘The Weaver of Winds’
Giants ‘The Up-World’
elves ‘The Fair-Roof’
The dwarfs ‘The Dripping Hall’
riddles.notes: Thor's question has a corrupt word (Bellows note 11; '† erakendi' in the Norse). Sky things are filed under 'weather'.

acquire.who: a skald at the king's seat
acquire.why: Skalds needed many names for one thing; he knows them by heart.

riddles.answer: What call they the moon, that men behold
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Thor's question, st. 13 (text t-alv-13)
clues: ‘Flame’ the gods among
‘The Wheel’ in the house of hell
‘The Goer’ the giants
‘The Gleamer’ the dwarfs
The elves ‘The Teller of Time’
riddles.notes: Compare Vafthruthnir's lay st. 23 and 25: the moon is made 'To tell the time for men'.

acquire.why: Skalds needed many names for one thing; he knows them by heart.

riddles.answer: What call they the sun, that all men see
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Thor's question, st. 15 (text t-alv-15)
clues: gods ‘Orb of the Sun’
‘The Deceiver of Dvalin’ the dwarfs
The giants ‘The Ever-Bright’
elves ‘Fair Wheel’
‘All-Glowing’ the sons of the gods
riddles.notes: Bellows note 16: the sun 'deceives' the dwarf Dvalin because sunlight turns dwarfs to stone; it is how Alvis dies (st. 35).

acquire.why: Skalds needed many names for one thing; he knows them by heart.

riddles.answer: What call they the clouds, that keep the rains
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Thor's question, st. 17 (text t-alv-17)
clues: ‘Rain-Hope’ gods call them
The Wanes call them ‘Kites of the Wind’
‘Water-Hope’ giants
‘Weather-Might’ elves
‘The Helmet of Secrets’ in hell

acquire.why: The names of the clouds are weather lore.

riddles.answer: What call they the wind, that widest fares
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Thor's question, st. 19 (text t-alv-19)
clues: the gods ‘The Waverer’
‘The Neigher’ the holy ones high
‘The Wailer’ the giants
‘Roaring Wender’ the elves
In hell ‘The Blustering Blast’
riddles.notes: Snorri quotes this stanza (Bellows note 20). For where the wind comes from, see Vafthruthnir's lay st. 37.

acquire.why: The names of the wind are a seaman's.

riddles.answer: What call they the calm, that quiet lies
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Thor's question, st. 21 (text t-alv-21)
clues: ‘The Quiet’ the gods
The Wanes ‘The Hush of the Winds’
‘The Sultry’ the giants
elves ‘Day’s Stillness’
The dwarfs ‘The Shelter of Day’
riddles.notes: A becalmed ship knows this one.

acquire.who: a Norse skipper becalmed beside you
acquire.why: The names of the calm are a seaman's.

riddles.answer: What call they the sea, whereon men sail
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Thor's question, st. 23 (text t-alv-23)
clues: gods ‘The Smooth-Lying’
‘The Wave’ is it called by the Wanes
‘Eel-Home’ the giants
‘Drink-Stuff’ the elves
For the dwarfs its name is ‘The Deep’
riddles.notes: Bellows note 24 doubts 'Drink-Stuff' (Gering's guess). The example in map_play_ideas.md ('Eel-Home') is from this stanza.

acquire.why: Skalds needed many names for one thing; he knows them by heart.

riddles.answer: What call they the fire, that flames for men
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Thor's question, st. 25 (text t-alv-25)
clues: ‘Flame’ the gods
By the Wanes is it ‘Wildfire’ called
‘The Biter’ by giants
‘The Burner’ by dwarfs
‘The Swift’ in the house of hell
riddles.notes: Bellows note 26: 'Wildfire' may also mean 'Wave'.

acquire.why: Skalds needed many names for one thing; he knows them by heart.

riddles.answer: What call they the wood, that grows for mankind
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Thor's question, st. 27 (text t-alv-27)
clues: gods ‘The Mane of the Field’
‘Seaweed of Hills’ in hell
‘Flame-Food’ the giants
‘Fair-Limbed’ the elves
‘The Wand’ is it called by the Wanes
riddles.notes: Timber as a good. Bellows note 28: the word read 'in hell' simply means 'men' (Norse 'halir').

acquire.who: a timber trader of the west
acquire.why: Wood is his trade.

riddles.answer: What call they the night, the daughter of Nor
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Thor's question, st. 29 (text t-alv-29)
clues: ‘Darkness’ gods name it
‘The Hood’ the holy ones high
The giants ‘The Lightless’
the elves ‘Sleep’s Joy’
The dwarfs ‘The Weaver of Dreams’
riddles.notes: Snorri quotes this stanza (Bellows note 30). Nor is the father of Night (Vafthruthnir's lay st. 25).

acquire.why: Skalds needed many names for one thing; he knows them by heart.

riddles.answer: What call they the seed, that is sown by men
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Thor's question, st. 31 (text t-alv-31)
clues: ‘Corn’ the gods
‘Growth’ in the world of the Wanes
‘The Eaten’ by giants
‘Drink-Stuff’ by elves
In hell ‘The Slender Stem’
riddles.notes: Bellows note 32: both words for 'grain' and 'corn' meant primarily barley. 'Drink-Stuff': grain as the stuff beer is brewed from (Gering's guess).

acquire.who: a farmer of the king's estate
acquire.why: Barley is his crop (the Danish isles grow it).

riddles.answer: What call they the ale, that is quaffed of men
riddles.answerSource: the poem: Thor's question, st. 33 (text t-alv-33)
clues: ‘Beer’ the gods among
In the world of the Wanes ‘The Foaming’
‘Bright Draught’ with giants
‘Mead’ with dwellers in hell
‘The Feast-Draught’ with Suttung’s sons
riddles.notes: Last of Thor's thirteen questions; in st. 35 the sun rises and the dwarf is caught. Links to Gestumblindi 1 (ale).

acquire.who: Ravn, when you answer the first riddle
acquire.why: The names of ale follow the riddle of ale.

riddles.answer: 'the Storm' (Dietrich: 'in 2, 3, 4, only a single subject is included, "the Storm"', quoted by Tupper 1910)
riddles.answerSource: scholars' agreement: Dietrich 1859 (Haupts Zeitschrift XI, 461), followed by Prehn, Brooke and Tupper 1910 (Notes, Riddle 2, scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 9783-9800)
clues: folcsalo bærne, ræced reafige (public structures burn, houses rob)
recas stigað haswe ofer hrofum (the smoke mounts dusky o'er the roofs)
ic wudu hrere ... beamas fylle (I shake the wood ... fell the trees)
hwa mec on sið wræce (who me on journey sends)
riddles.notes: Part 1 of a three-part set (texts exeter_01, exeter_02, exeter_03): Dietrich read them as one subject seen on land, under the sea and in the sky. Good as a multi-part riddle whose pieces are found in different places. Aldhelm's 'Ventus' (aldhelm_02_ventus) is the Latin cousin: Ehwald's note links it to this riddle. Thorpe printed a full stop after 'thunder'; kept as printed. OCR note: Thorpe's italic 'I' reads as '/' in the scan and is given as 'I'.

acquire.who: a monk of the scriptorium; later, a minster priest at York
acquire.why: Minsters copied English riddle verse (the Exeter Book is one such book, c. 970).

riddles.answerSource: scholars' agreement: Dietrich 1859; Tupper 1910 (Notes, Riddle 2-3). Grein 1858 had guessed 'Anchor', which Tupper calls 'an impossible solution'.
clues: under yþa geþræc eorþan secan, garsecges grund (under the rush of waves, seeking the earth, the ocean's ground)
hwælmere hlimmeð (the whale-mere resounds)
streamas staþu beatað (streams beat the shores)
riddles.notes: Part 2 of the storm set. Answer is the same thing as part 1: a chain where the first answer unlocks the second. Thorpe's asterisk (an untranslated word, 'stealc') is kept as printed.

acquire.who: a monk of the scriptorium; later, the king's gleeman
acquire.why: Minsters copied English riddle verse; gleemen sang it in hall.

riddles.answer: 'the Storm' (earthquake, sea-storm and thunderstorm in turn) (Dietrich, quoted by Tupper 1910)
riddles.answerSource: scholars' agreement: Dietrich 1859 ('first ... an earthquake; then, as driver of waves and assailant of ships; finally as cloud-farer and thunderstorm'), quoted by Tupper 1910, Notes p. 69 (?) (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 9785-9796); Grein 1858 'Hurricane'
clues: þær bið ceole wen sliþre sæcce (there shall be hope for the vessel in the fierce contest)
won wægfatu (the dark wave-vessel)
þurh regn ufan ... stræle fleogan (through rain from above ... the arrow fly)
wolcnfare wrege (the clouds' course drive)
riddles.notes: Part 3 of the storm set; the longest piece and the most useful to a sea trader (ships driven onto cliffs in a storm). Tupper also compares Eusebius 23 'De aequore' (eusebius_23_aequore).

acquire.who: a leaf in a sea chest washed ashore
acquire.why: Storms wrecked many ships in the British sea (799, in the chronicle); a leaf survives in a chest.

riddles.answerSource: scholars' agreement: L. C. Müller, Collectanea Anglo-Saxonica 1835; Dietrich 1859 (XI, 461); Prehn; Tupper 1910, Notes p. 80 (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 10423-10430; Trautmann's 'chopping-block' rejected)
clues: iserne wund, bille gebennad (with iron wounded, with faulchion scar'd)
Oft ic wig seo (oft I battle see)
Næfre læcecynn ... wunde gehælde (never the healing tribe ... my wounds would heal)
riddles.notes: Tupper notes the shield also speaks of its wounds in the 26th riddle of Hervarar saga: a link to the Norse riddle set.

acquire.who: a thegn of the king's hall
acquire.why: A warrior's riddle about his shield.

riddles.answer: 'the sun' (the S-rune, sigel 'the sun', stands before and after the riddle in the manuscript)
riddles.answerSource: the manuscript's own rune mark and scholars' agreement: Tupper 1910, Notes, Riddle 7 ('putting the solution beyond doubt'; scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 10494-10497)
clues: oft ic cwice bærne (oft I the living burn)
swa ic him no hrine (yet I touch them not)
ofer deop gedreag (over the deep abyss)
riddles.notes: A game version could show the S-rune ᛋ beside the text as the manuscript does, as a hard extra clue.

acquire.why: Bede's house at Jarrow reckoned the course of sun and moon.

riddles.answerSource: scholars' agreement: Tupper 1910, Notes, Riddle 8 (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 10551-10553)
clues: Hrægl min swigað (my garment sounds)
oþþe wado drefe (or the waters drive)
Frætwe mine swogað hlude (my ornaments sound loudly)
riddles.notes: The singing feathers are the wild swan's wingbeat, heard on the North Sea coasts in winter.

acquire.why: He hears the swans' wings in winter.

riddles.answer: 'Cuckoo' (Dietrich; Tupper: 'has been accepted by all scholars')
riddles.answerSource: scholars' agreement: Dietrich 1859 (XI, 463); Tupper 1910, Notes, Riddle 10 (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt line 10764)
clues: deadne ofgeafun fæder ond modor (gave up as dead, father and mother)
swa hire agen bearn (as her own child)
heo hæfde swæsra þy læs suna ond dohtra (she had the less of her own sons and daughters)
riddles.notes: The 'dead' one left behind is the egg. Tupper notes a link to Symphosius 100 (not in the best manuscripts).

acquire.why: A country riddle of spring.

riddles.answerSource: scholars' agreement: Stopford Brooke, Early English Literature 1892, p. 179; accepted by Tupper 1910, Notes, Riddle 11 (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 10885-10888); Dietrich had guessed 'anchor'
clues: Neb wæs min on nearwe (my face was in constraint)
liþendum wuda (to sailors in ships / to floating wood)
þa ic of fæðmum cwom brimes ond beames (when I from the clutches came of sea and ship)
ofer seolhbaþo (over the seal's baths)
riddles.notes: Rests on the medieval belief that barnacle geese grow from shells on driftwood (Tupper quotes Giraldus Cambrensis). Hard: the merchant must have heard that sailors' tale. Thorpe misread 'liþendum wuda' as 'sailors in ships'.

acquire.why: The tale that these geese grow on driftwood is told round the Irish Sea (?).

riddles.answer: 'Oxhide' or 'Leather' (Tupper: 'the answer accepted by all authorities')
riddles.answerSource: scholars' agreement: Tupper 1910, Notes p. 93, Riddle 13 (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 11159-11160)
clues: Fotum ic fere, foldan slite (on feet I go, the earth tear)
Gif me feorh losað, fæste binde swearte Wealas (if my life perish, fast I bind the swart strangers)
ic lifgende lond reafige ond æfter deaþe dryhtum þeowige (I who living rob the land, and after death multitudes serve)
riddles.notes: FLAG: lines 9-13 (the drunken serving woman, 'hygegalan hond', a wanton hand) are a double meaning; the answer itself is innocent. The living ox ploughs; its hide becomes leather bonds, bottles and shoes. Ox and leather are both in the trade world; accept either the animal or the leather. Tupper links it to Eusebius 37 and Symphosius 56.

acquire.why: The ox's hide is his trade.

riddles.answerSource: scholars' agreement (later): Tupper 1910, Notes p. 96-97, Riddle 14 (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 11377-11393), against older guesses (butterfly cocoon, the alphabet); the answer is now standard (?)
clues: tyn wæron ealra, six gebroþor ond hyra sweostor mid (ten they were in all, six brethren, and their sisters)
Fell hongedon ... on seles wæge (the skins hung on the room's wall)
Hrægl bið geniwad (clothing is renew'd)
riddles.notes: The 'skins' are the eggshells, the new 'clothing' their feathers. Very hard. Tupper says he solved it himself in Modern Language Notes; the solution is the accepted one today, but mark (?) on 'agreed by all'.

acquire.why: A farmyard riddle.

riddles.answer: 'Horn' (Dietrich: 'Das horn redet ... von sich als einstigem kampfer')
riddles.answerSource: scholars' agreement: Dietrich 1859 (XI, 464); Tupper 1910, Notes p. 98, Riddle 15 (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 11478-11484)
clues: Ic wæs wæpenwiga (I was an armed warrior)
hwilum merehengest fereð ofer flodas (sometimes the sea-horse conveys me o'er the floods)
wlitig on wage þær weras drincað (splendid on the wall, where men drink)
þonne ic winde sceal ... swelgan (then with wind I must swell)
riddles.notes: Both drinking horn and blowing horn: one answer. 'merehengest' (sea-stallion) is a kenning for ship: a kennings lesson inside a riddle. Horn is a trade good.

acquire.why: He makes drinking and blowing horns.

riddles.answerSource: scholars' agreement: Dietrich 1859 (XI, 465), accepted by Prehn, Brooke, McLean, Cosijn and Tupper 1910, Notes p. 101, Riddle 16 (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 11661-11666); Walz and Holthausen argued for porcupine or hedgehog
clues: Hals is min hwit ond heafod fealo (my neck is white, and my head dun)
þurh steapne beorg stræte wyrcan (through a steep mountain work a road)
þurh dune þyrel (through a dim hole)
riddles.notes: Mostly agreed; a minority prefer hedgehog or porcupine. Accept badger.

acquire.why: A hunter's riddle.

riddles.answerSource: scholars' agreement: Dietrich 1859 (XI, 452); Tupper 1910, Notes p. 104, Riddle 17 (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt line 11828)
clues: wiþ wæge winnan ond wiþ winde feohtan (with the wave I must contend, and against the wind fight)
eorþan yþum þeaht (the earth with billows cover'd)
gif min steort þolað (if my tail suffers)
stanas moton fæste gehabban (against the stones they can fast retain)
riddles.notes: Source: Symphosius 61 'Ancora' (symphosius_61_ancora): a chain, the Latin title gives away the English answer to a merchant who can read Latin. A ship's thing every merchant knows.

acquire.who: the master of an English ship you hail
acquire.why: Ship's gear is every seaman's riddle.

riddles.answerSource: the runes in the text, read backwards (Thorpe 1842, note p. 527, scratchpad\thorpe_exon.txt line 64863); Tupper 1910, Notes p. 108, Riddle 20 (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 12039-12045). riddles.answerSource: scholars' agreement: Dietrich 1859 (XI, 465), accepted by Brooke; Tupper 1910, Notes p. 109, Riddle 21 (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 12181-12186); Trautmann's 'hawk' rejected
clues: hondweorc smiþa (hand-work of smiths)

riddles.answer: 'By this, no doubt, a plough is intended.' (Thorpe 1842); 'Plow' (Dietrich)
riddles.answerSource: Thorpe 1842, note p. 527 (scratchpad\thorpe_exon.txt line 64873); Tupper 1910, Notes p. 113, Riddle 22: 'Dietrich's answer ... has been generally accepted' (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 12361-12362)
clues: Neb is min niþerweard (my face is downward)
be grunde græfe (along the ground dig)
grene on healfe ... sweart on oþre (green on one side ... black on the other)
hongaþ under an orþoncpil (hangs beneath one curious dart)
riddles.notes: One of the two Exeter riddles Thorpe himself solved in 1842.

acquire.why: His own tool.

riddles.answer: 'Bow' (the opening word Agof read backwards; Tupper: 'this "Bow" riddle')
riddles.answerSource: the text itself ('Agof is min noma eft onhwyrfed', Agof is my name transposed) and scholars' agreement: Tupper 1910, Notes p. 119, Riddle 24 (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt line 12695)

þonne ic onbuge (when I bend)
þæt me of hrife fleogeð (what from my belly flies)

acquire.why: His own work.

hwilum beorce swa hund (sometimes I bark as a dog)
ᚷ ᚫ ᚱ ᚩ ᚻ ᛁ ... swa þa siex stafas sweotule becnaþ (as those six letters plainly indicate)

baþedan in bydene (bathed in a tub)

riddles.answerSource: scholars' agreement: Dietrich 1859 (XI, 468-469), Prehn, Brooke 1892; Tupper 1910, Notes p. 137, Riddle 30 (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 13807-13808)

deaw feol on eorþan, niht forð gewat (dew fell on earth, night departed forth)
riddles.notes: The horned moon carries off light as plunder; the sun takes it back at dawn. A raid in the sky: a fit riddle for a trader who knows raiders. Hard: two answers at once.

sceal on anum fet (must on one foot: the keel)

riddles.notes: Best fit for the game: a merchant ship bringing food and paying its yearly due. Tupper explains the one foot as the keel, the ribs as the frames, the mouth as the hatch to the hold.

Is min modor ... þæt is dohtor min (my mother ... she is my daughter: ice and water)
riddles.notes: The 'mother who is also my daughter' (water makes ice, ice makes water) is an old riddle motif; Tupper traces it in Aldhelm's letter and Bede. Pairs with exeter_68_69_ice, Symphosius 'Glacies' and Tatwine 'De nive, grandine et glacie'. A danger to ships in the north.

þeof in þystro (a thief in darkness)
Stælgiest ne wæs wihte þy gleawra (the stealing guest was not in aught the wiser)
riddles.notes: The text names the moth; the thing to find is what it eats: the book. Accept 'bookworm' or 'moth'. CHAIN: Symphosius 16 'Tinea' (symphosius_16_tinea) is the source.

acquire.why: He fights moths among the books.

riddles.answerSource: scholars' agreement: Dietrich 1859 (XI, 480) 'Ice', Grein 'Winter'; Tupper 1910, Notes p. 208, Riddle 69: 'Though Dietrich is certainly right' (scratchpad\m2\riddlesofexeterbook00tuppuoft.txt lines 17878-17884)
clues: Wundor wearð on wege (a wonder was on the way: on the waves)

riddles.notes: The shortest riddle in the set and one of the hardest. Thorpe's English is wrong here: he took 'bane' (bone) as 'bane' and wrote 'water was turn'd to poison'. Tupper reads the two opening lines and the last line as one riddle; Thorpe and Krapp & Dobbie print them as two.

acquire.why: Toll-reeves reckoned on wax tablets (?).

riddles.answer: 'Oyster' (Tupper: 'Dietrich is doubtless right in his answer')

feþelease (footless)

riddles.notes: Thorpe read the first words as 'He who produced me' (taking 'se' as 'he'), not 'the sea'. The end of the riddle is burnt away in the manuscript. Oysters are a coastal food trade.

acquire.why: The oysters of Richborough were famous since Roman times.
